To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have engineered zinc finger recombinase enzymes with adaptable DNA sequence specificity.

we have engineered zinc finger recombinase (ZFR) enzymes with DNA sequence specificities for 3 different 9 bp sites, and have used them to promote site-specific integration of a 2.1 kb DNA fragment at 3 different 22 bp "Z-sites", in the presence of an asymmetric Z-site.
we have engineered zinc finger recombinase proteins with DNA binding domains that can recognize any sequence in the genome.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel type of site-specific recombinase, based on zinc finger proteins, for use in biotechnology.
the development of new technologies for the manipulation of genes in plants.
the design of new tools to manipulate the genomes of plants, animals and microorganisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

zinc finger recombinase technology has the potential to revolutionise the field of site-specific recombination, allowing the precise excision of DNA sequences from natural genomes and the targeted insertion of foreign DNA sequences.
ZFRs are a new generation of recombinases with the potential to revolutionize the field of molecular genetics.
ZFRs have the ability to promote site specific recombination at many DNA sequences.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the zinc finger recombinase technology has been successfully used to create a new class of site specific recombinases that are able to target sequences that are not recognized by naturally occurring site specific recombinase.
ZFRs are a promising technology to target DNA recombination in a site-specific manner.

we have shown that the ZFRs can mediate site-specific recombination between two Z-sites, that the recombination can be asymmetric, and that it can be directed by the ZFR to a heterologous recombination site.
The main takeaway from our work is that
ZFRs with the appropriate specificity can be designed to promote recombination between two sites in a target sequence, even when the two sites are asymmetric.
the zinc finger recombinase technology has the potential to be a general method for targeted DNA recombination, with applications in biotechnology, gene therapy and synthetic biology.
the Z-sites are not just a theoretical construct but a useful and practical tool for site-specific genome editing.
